headline: Rhode Island adds three lenders to first-time homebuyer program after 119 purchases
dek: The third phase of RI AnchorHome expands the lender network after the state-backed program financed more than $45 million in first-home purchases, even as Rhode Island prices remain out of reach for many buyers.
body: Rhode Island is expanding its RI AnchorHome mortgage program to three additional lenders after the initiative helped finance 119 first-time home purchases totaling more than $45 million, state Treasurer James Diossa announced Tuesday. BayCoast Bank, Bristol County Savings Bank and Westerly Community Credit Union will join the program as it enters a third phase. The announcement came from the [Rhode Island Office of the General Treasurer](https://treasury.ri.gov/press-releases/treasurer-diossa-announces-ri-anchorhome-expansion-after-helping-more-100-rhode).

The expansion is aimed at widening access rather than replacing the private mortgage market. Under RI AnchorHome, an eligible first-time buyer applies through a participating bank or credit union. If the lender approves the mortgage, the state deposits matching funds at that institution. The lender still issues and services the loan; the state is not the borrower’s mortgage company. Treasury says the structure gives participating institutions more room to offer affordable terms while keeping lending decisions with the financial institution.

The program’s headline terms are a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage with a starting interest rate of 3.99%, subject to market conditions, and no private mortgage insurance. Buyers may also use down-payment and closing-cost assistance, and homeownership counseling is required. Those terms are significant for households trying to manage the upfront cost of a purchase, but the program is not a universal subsidy: buyers must meet the program’s first-time-homebuyer and lender requirements, and an advertised starting rate can change with market conditions.

The three original participating institutions were Navigant Credit Union, Centreville Bank and BankNewport. The new lenders add geographic and institutional reach to a program that began in December 2025. [What's Up Newp](https://whatsupnewp.com/2026/10/states-first-time-homebuyer-program-adds-three-lenders-after-financing-119-purchases/) reported that the average RI AnchorHome loan is about $383,000, while the average purchase price for the financed homes is just above $400,000. Those figures describe the program’s borrowers to date; they are not a statewide home-price average or a promise that every applicant will receive the same loan size.

The timing reflects the gap between the program’s growing use and Rhode Island’s broader affordability problem. HousingWorks RI Executive Director Brenda Clement, cited in the independent report, said the state’s median single-family home price had risen 5.3% to $499,900 and that average rent for a two-bedroom apartment had reached $2,358. The figures help explain why a lower-cost mortgage pathway may matter, while also showing its limits: a program that has financed 119 purchases is operating within a housing market where the typical home costs more than the average AnchorHome purchase.

RI AnchorHome uses public deposits through the state’s Community Deposit Program and operates under the oversight of the State Investment Commission. Treasury’s program information says the deposits are collateralized and subject to safety, liquidity and reporting requirements. The state is leveraging its financial position to influence the terms available through private lenders, not directly taking ownership risk on the homes or guaranteeing that a buyer will be approved.

For prospective buyers, the next step is to contact one of the participating lenders and review eligibility, income limits, loan limits and counseling requirements before relying on the advertised rate. Treasury’s [program page](https://treasury.ri.gov/programs/anchorhome) says RI AnchorHome is for first-time buyers purchasing a primary residence in Rhode Island and lists maximum loan amounts of $525,000 for a single-family home and $575,000 for a two-family home. It also says household income is capped at 110% of statewide income limits and that a borrower cannot own another residential property at closing.

The state’s announcement did not set a deadline for the new lenders to begin taking applications, so availability may depend on each institution’s rollout. What is clear is the policy direction: Rhode Island is adding private partners after an initial group of lenders moved more than 100 buyers into homeownership, while officials present the state-deposit model as one tool for a market where rents and home prices continue to pressure working households. The program’s results will be measured not only by the number of additional lenders, but by whether qualified buyers can actually close on homes they can sustain over time.
